'''avaricious''' (av-ạ-rish′us), ''a.'' [< ME. ''avaricious'', < F. ''avaricieux'', < ''avarice''. Cf. ''avarous''.] Characterized by avarice; greedy of gain; immoderately desirous of accumulating property; eager to acquire or possess.
{{smaller block|Luxurious, ''avaricious'', false, deceitful.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3.}}
Liberal of everything else, he [Walpole] was ''avaricious'' of power.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Horace Walpole.}}}}

'''avariciously''' (av-ạ-rish′us-li), ''adv.'' In an avaricious manner; with inordinate desire of gaining wealth; covetously.
{{smaller block|Each is contented with his own possessions, nor ''avariciously'' endeavours to heap up more than is necessary for his own subsistence.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Essays, xvi.}}}}

'''avariciousness''' (av-ạ-rish′us-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being avaricious; insatiable or inordinate passion for property.

'''avarous†''', ''a.'' [ME. ''avarous'', ''averous'', < OF. ''averos'', ''averus'' (extended form as if < ''aver'', possession: see ''aver''<sup>2</sup>); cf. ''aver'', ''avar'', mod. F. ''avare'', < L. ''avarus'', greedy: see ''avarice''.] Covetous; avaricious: as, “the erle ''avarous'',” ''Piers Plowman''.

'''avast''' (ạ-väst′), ''interj.'' [Prob. < D. ''hou’ vast'', ''houd vast'' = E. ''hold fast'', i. e., hold on, wait a while. Cf. D. ''houvast'' = E. ''holdfast'', a cramp-iron.] ''Naut.'', stop! hold! cease! stay! [Sometimes used colloquially.]
{{smaller block|''Avast'' hailing! Don’t you know me, mother Partlett?
{{right|''Cumberland.''}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|avail|392|avast}}</noinclude>But how out of this can she ''avail?''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To be for the advantage of; assist or profit: as, what will skill ''avail'' us against numbers?
{{smaller block|Yet all this ''availeth'' me nothing. {{right|Esther v. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|All the songs and newspapers and money-subscriptions and vituperations of such as do not think with us, will ''avail'' nothing against a fact.
{{right|''Emerson'', West Indian Emancipation.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>“God save us!” cried the captain,
“For naught can man ''avail.''”</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The Mantle of St. John De Matha.}}}}
'''2†.''' To promote; prosper; assist: said of things.
{{smaller block|<poem>Meantime he voyaged to explore the will
Of Jove on high Dodona’s holy hill,
What means might best his safe return ''avail.'' ''Pope.''</poem>}}
'''3.''' To advantage; profit; give the benefit to: used reflexively, with ''of'': as, he ''availed himself of'' the opportunity. [Often used colloquially in the United States without the pronoun.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Then shall they seek t’ ''avail themselves of'' names,
Places and titles. ''Milton'', P. L., xii. 515.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|The theatre ''avails itself of'' the best talent of poet, of painter, and of amateur of taste, to make the ensemble of dramatic effect. {{right|''Emerson'', Misc., p. 396.}}}}
'''To avail one’s self by†''', to avail one’s self of.
{{smaller block|And my peculiar profit persuaded me, sometimes, to ''avail myself by'' their folly. {{right|''Sanford.''}}}}

'''avail<sup>1</sup>''' (a-vāl′), ''n.''   [< ME. ''availe'', < ''availen'': see ''avail'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' Advantage, profit, or benefit, in a general sense; also, value or estimation. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|The ''avail'' of a death-bed repentance. {{right|''Jer. Taylor.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Thy pardon; I but speak for thine ''avail.''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Gareth and Lynette.}}}}
'''2.''' Efficacy for a purpose; advantage to an object or end: now used chiefly in negative phrases, or sentences of negative import: as, of little or no ''avail;'' I doubt whether it will be of much ''avail.''
{{smaller block|<poem>But Cranstoun’s lance, of more ''avail'',
Pierced through, like silk, the Borderer’s mail;
Through shield, and jack, and acton passed.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., iii. 6.}}}}
'''3.''' ''pl.'' Profits or proceeds: as, the ''avails'' of a sale by auction.{{smaller|—'''Avail of marriage''', in ''Scots law'', a sum payable to the superior by the heir of a deceased ward-vassal on his becoming marriageable.}}='''Syn. 1''' {{smaller|and '''2.''' Use, utility, service.—'''3.''' Returns.}}

'''avail<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v.'' See ''avale.''

'''availability''' (a̤-vā-la̤-bil′i-ti), ''n.''   [< ''available'': see ''-bility.'']   The state of being available; suitableness for the accomplishment of a given purpose; capability of advantageous use or employment: as, the ''availability'' of a candidate for office, or of a proposed method.

'''available''' (a̤-vā′la̤-bl), ''a.''   [< ME. ''avaylable;'' < ''avail''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able.'']   '''1.''' Profitable; advantageous; having efficacy.
{{smaller block|Those who will consult him [Fourier] for no other reason, might do so to see how the energies of Woman may be made ''available'' in the pecuniary way.
{{right|''Marg. Fuller'', Woman in 19th Cent., p. 124.}}}}
'''2.''' Having sufficient power, force, or efficacy for the object; valid. {{smaller block|Laws human are ''available'' by consent. {{right|''Hooker.''}}}}
{{smaller block|She knows no commendation is more ''available'' with thee than that of proper virtue.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, v. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' Capable of being used or employed with advantage; attainable; accessible; at one’s disposal: as, his resources were not ''available'' at the time.
{{smaller block|The whole army is called 700,000 men, but of these only 80,000 can be reckoned ''available.'' {{right|''Brougham.''}}}}
{{smaller block|We do not choose our own candidate, no, nor any other man’s first choice,—but only the ''available'' candidate, whom, perhaps, no man loves. {{right|''Emerson'', Misc., p. 401.}}}}
''Advailable'' is a rare and obsolete form.

'''availableness''' (a̤-vā′la̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state of being available; capability of being used; power or efficacy in promoting an end in view. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The efficacy, or ''availableness'', . . . or suitableness of these reductives to the end proposed.
{{right|''Sir M. Hale'', Orig. of Mankind, p. 225.}}}}
'''2.''' Competent power; legal force; validity: as, the ''availableness'' of a title.

'''availably''' (a̤-vā′la̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an available manner; so as to be used with efficacy; profitably; advantageously; validly; efficaciously.

'''availingly''' (a̤-vā′ling-li), ''adv.'' In an availing manner; successfully.
{{smaller block|It [the Bible] is worshipped with a positive idolatry, in extenuation of whose gross fanaticism its intrinsic beauty pleads ''availingly'' with the man of letters and the scholar.
{{right|''Faber'', in Dublin Rev., June, 1853.}}}}

'''availment''' (a̤-vāl′ment), ''n.''   [< ''avail''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', + ''-ment.'']   Profit; efficacy; successful issue.   ''Bailey.'' [Rare.]

'''aval'''<sup>1</sup> (ā′vạl), ''a.''   [< L. ''avus'', grandfather, + ''-al.'']   Relating to grandparents.
{{smaller block|The rare opportunities of authentic verification of special parental or ''aval'' recollections.
{{right|''Science'', III. 345.}}}}

'''aval'''<sup>2</sup> (a-val′), ''n.''   [F., an indorsement, guaranty, < ''à val'', at the bottom: see ''avale''.]   In Canada, an act of suretyship or guaranty on a promissory note.

'''avalanche''' (av′a-lȧnch), ''n.''   [< F. ''avalanche'' (also ''avalange''), dial. form (Swiss ''evalanche'') of *''avalance'' (ML. ''avalantia''), lit. descent, < ''avaler'', let fall down: see ''avale'' and ''-ance''.]   '''1.''' The fall or sliding down of a mass of snow or ice from a mountain-slope. {{smaller|The sliding down of ordinary snow is, in high snow-covered mountains, an event of frequent occurrence, and is generally not dangerous or destructive, since it mostly takes place high above habitations and forests. Partly consolidated snow, or névé, however, is sometimes set in motion in large quantities, and such an occurrence may be productive of very serious injury, especially to the forests below. Small glaciers sometimes detach themselves from their rocky beds and fall into the valley below; such events are rare, but have sometimes been attended by very disastrous results. The more terrible catastrophes which have occurred, and by which, especially in the Alps, whole villages have been buried, have been due to the sliding down of a portion of the rock itself of which the mountain was formed. These “rock-avalanches,” as they are sometimes called, are more properly denominated land-slips or land-slides. See ''land-slip'', ''land-slide''.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Around his [Mont Blanc’s] waist are forests braced,
The ''avalanche'' in his hand;
But ere it fall, that thundering ball</poem> Must pause at my command. {{right|''Byron'', Manfred, i. 1.}}}}
Hence —'''2.''' Anything resembling an avalanche in suddenness and destructiveness: as, an ''avalanche'' of misfortunes.

'''avale†''' (a-vāl′), ''v.''   [< ME. ''avalen'', ''auvalen'', < OF. ''avaler'', ''availer'' (= Pr. ''avalar'' = OIt. ''avallare''), come down, let down, < ''a val'', downward, < L. ''ad vallem'', lit. to the valley: ''ad'', to; ''vallem'', acc. of ''valles'', valley, vale: see ''vale''. Cf. ''amount'', < L. ''ad montem'', to the hill; ''down'', ''adown'', < AS. ''of dūne'', from the hill.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To come down; fall.
{{smaller block|<poem>A rayn from hevene gan ''avale''.</poem>{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 626.}}}}
'''2.''' To descend; dismount.
{{smaller block|They . . . from their sweaty Coursers did ''avale''.{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ix. 10.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To lower; uncover; take off, as a vizor or hood.   ''Chaucer.''
{{smaller block|Hodid men were cleped thanne the Lolardis, that wold never ''avale'' here hood in presens of the Sacrament.{{right|''Capgrave’s Chron.'', p. 245, an. 1387. Quoted in G. P.}}{{right|[Marsh’s Hist. Eng. Lang., p. 7.}}}}
'''2.''' To let down; lower, as a sail; cause to descend: as, “hath his saile ''avaled'',” ''Gower'', Conf. Amant., viii.
{{smaller block|<poem>By that, the welked Phœbus gan ''availe''
His weary waine. {{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., Jan.}}</poem>
<poem>Thou seest my lowly saile,
That froward fortune doth ever ''availe''.</poem>{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., Sept.}}}}
'''3.''' To make low or abject; depress; degrade.

'''avant-garde†''' (ạ-vänt′gärd; F. pron. a-voṅ′gärd), ''n.''   [< F. ''avant-garde'', < ''avant'', before, + garde'', guard: see ''vanguard''.]   Advance-guard.

'''avantplat''' (a-voṅ′plä), ''n.'' Same as ''vamplate.''

'''avanturin, avanturine''' (ạ-van′t̮ụ̄-rin), ''n.'' and ''a.'' See ''aventurin.''

'''avarice''' (av′a̤-ris), ''n.''   [< ME. ''avarice'', < OF. ''avarice'' (F. ''avarice''), < L. ''avaritia'', < ''avarus'', greedy (cf. ''avidus'', avid: see ''avid''), < ''avēre'', wish, desire.]   An inordinate desire of gaining and possessing wealth; covetousness; cupidity; greediness, or insatiable desire of gain.
{{smaller block|<poem>So for a good old-gentlemanly vice
I think I must take up with ''avarice.''</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, i. 216.}}}}
{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' ''Avarice, Covetousness, Cupidity'', penuriousness, closeness, miserliness, all denote bad qualities, corruptions of the natural instinct of possession. ''Avarice'', literally greediness, a strong desire to get objects of value, has become limited, except in figurative uses, so as to express only a sordid and mastering desire to get wealth. ''Covetousness'' and ''cupidity'' are not limited to wealth, but may have for their object anything that can be desired, ''cupidity'' being directed especially toward material things. ''Covetousness'' longs to possess that which belongs to another; hence the prohibition in the tenth commandment (Ex. xx. 17). ''Cupidity'' is more active than the others, less groveling, and more ready to snatch from others that which ''covetousness'' may wish for without trying to get. See ''penurious.''}}
{{smaller block|<poem>There grows,
In my most ill-compos’d affection, such
A stanchless ''avarice'', that, were I king,
I should cut off the nobles for their lands.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|I would not have you to think that my desire of having is the sin of ''covetousness.'' {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|When this continent was first discovered, it became an object of ''cupidity'' to the ambition of many of the nations of Europe. {{right|''Story'', Speech, Salem, Sept. 18, 1828.}}}}
